sentences.text: The genus name Ornithoprion translates from Greek as 'bird saw', referring to the bird-like skull and saw-like lower jaw teeth. This creature possessed a lower jaw tooth arrangement called a tooth whorl, which looked like a saw and featured up to seven broad, rounded tooth crowns.

The specific name hertwigi honors the German zoologist Oscar Hertwig. Many dermal denticles on Ornithoprion fused into compound scales called polyodontode scales, featuring a single base with up to seven crowns.

Most known specimens are preserved on their side and are flattened, including the holotype. The mandibular rostrum articulated with the Meckel's cartilages at a flexible joint. Due to the shape of the Meckel's cartilages, the mouth of Ornithoprion was likely incapable of closing.
Ornithoprion's unfused pectoral girdles included an unpaired cartilaginous structure tentatively identified as sternal cartilage.
Bite marks and damage on some fossils indicate that Ornithoprion was preyed upon by other carnivores.
Zangerl suggested that the armor and jaw articulation of Ornithoprion's skull were shock-absorbing adaptations.
The genus Ornithoprion was described by Rainer Zangerl in 1966. The genus Ornithoprion and its type species O. hertwigi were formally described in 1966 by paleontologist Rainer Zangerl.
Specimen FMNH PF-2710 from the Mecca Quarry was designated as the holotype of the species. The study of the holotype and paratypes of Ornithoprion was primarily performed using radiographic imaging.

The only known species, Ornithoprion hertwigi, lived during the Moscovian stage of the Pennsylvanian subperiod. Fossils of Ornithoprion are preserved in black shales from the area that is now the Midwestern United States. All known specimens of Ornithoprion are preserved in carbonaceous shale.

The rounded shape of Ornithoprion's teeth suggests it hunted hard-shelled invertebrates. Ornithoprion is believed to have been durophagous, feeding on shelled invertebrates. The rounded, bulbous crowns of Ornithoprion's tooth whorl were likely adaptations for crushing shelled prey.
Most other fish skeletons from the Logan Quarry show similar feeding traces or are preserved in fossilized regurgitates or coprolites.

Ornithoprion is a distant relative of living sharks, despite sometimes being referred to as a shark. Ornithoprion was originally classified in the family Edestidae, which was traditionally placed in the order Bradyodonti or the subclass Holocephali. Zangerl originally classified Ornithoprion and other edestids as elasmobranchs.
In 1981, Zangerl reclassified Ornithoprion into the family Caseodontidae, superfamily Caseodontoidea, and order Eugeneodontiformes. Ornithoprion is classified within the family Caseodontidae.
Ornithoprion is classified in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the family Caseodontidae, though its classification has been debated due to its unique anatomy.
Ornithoprion lived during the Carboniferous period approximately 315.2 million years ago. Ornithoprion fossils were found in deposits from the North American Midcontinent Sea, a large inland sea.
Later work by Rainer Zangerl suggested that many chondrichthyans found with Ornithoprion, including eugeneodonts, were pelagic fishes that migrated into shallow waters.
While Zangerl speculated that processes on the back of the cranium were a fused hyoid arch, this interpretation has been questioned by paleontologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen.

There is a debate regarding the attachment of Ornithoprion's upper teeth, with some researchers suggesting they attached to the underside of the cranium while others believe they attached to a fused portion of the palatoquadrates.

Roger S. Miles tentatively placed Ornithoprion in Holocephali but suggested its similarities to edestids resulted from convergent evolution due to differences in gill anatomy, tooth histology, and palatoquadrates.

While Zangerl's family and order classifications are still used, his view that eugeneodonts are elasmobranchs has been refuted; they are now considered a monophyletic group within Holocephali. Some authors debate whether the shales containing Ornithoprion were formed in shallow water or deep-water environments.
